description_ru: Рассказ о поездке по исландской Кольцевой дороге: водопады, ледники, горячие источники и погода, которая меняется каждые десять минут.
text:
There is only one road that goes all the way around Iceland, and it is called Route One. It is about thirteen hundred kilometres long, mostly paved, and it passes within sight of waterfalls, volcanoes, glaciers and a great many sheep. Most visitors drive it in a week, although the locals will tell you that a month is not too long. I had ten days, a small rented car and a guidebook whose first page said, in capital letters, that the weather would change.

It certainly did. On the first morning in the capital, Reykjavik, it was sunny. By lunch, there was hail, and by the time I reached the south coast, a rainbow was stretched across a field of black rocks. The Icelanders have a saying that if you do not like the weather, you should wait five minutes. I learned to keep a waterproof jacket, sunglasses and a woolly hat on the passenger seat at all times, and I often used all three before breakfast.

The south coast is the most popular section, and for good reason. Seljalandsfoss is a waterfall that falls from a cliff in a single ribbon, and a path leads behind it, so that you can look at the landscape through a curtain of water. You will get wet, and you will not mind. A little further east, Skogafoss is wider and louder, and people say that a treasure chest is hidden behind it, left by a Viking settler. According to the legend, a boy once found the chest, but he was able to pull out only the ring before the rest was lost.

Farther along the road, the land turns to black sand and the ocean looks angry. At Reynisfjara, enormous waves reach much further up the beach than they appear to, and visitors have been swept away by them. A sign at the entrance warns tourists never to turn their backs on the sea, and I noticed that a guide was explaining the same thing to a group of teenagers, who were clearly more interested in their phones. Nobody argued with the sea that day, and everyone went home dry.

The most unforgettable stop was a glacier lagoon in the south-east. Huge pieces of ice break off the front of a glacier and drift slowly across a lake, in shades of blue, white and grey, before floating out to the Atlantic through a short channel. On the beach nearby, the smaller pieces wash up like diamonds on the black sand. I stood there for an hour in the wind, and when a seal lifted its head out of the water, I forgot that my fingers had gone numb.

The east of the country is quieter, with long fjords and little fishing villages, and the road sometimes climbs through mountain passes where the fog is so thick that you can barely see the car in front. Here I was reminded of a lesson that every driver in Iceland has to learn. Many bridges have only one lane, and the rule is that whoever arrives first has the right of way. Gravel roads are common as well, and the rental companies insist that you should drive slowly, because stones fly up and break windscreens.

In the north, the landscape becomes almost otherworldly. Near Lake Myvatn, steam rises from cracks in the ground, pools of mud bubble and the air smells of boiled eggs, because of the sulphur. Iceland sits on the boundary between two tectonic plates, which are slowly moving apart, and the heat from below is used to warm houses and to supply much of the country's electricity. In one café, I was served bread that had been baked underground in hot soil, and I was assured that it was perfectly safe.

Of course, nothing is more typical of Iceland than a hot spring. In the evenings, the locals gather in outdoor pools, which are heated by natural water and are surprisingly cheap, and talk about politics, football and the weather. There is one rule that surprises foreigners: you must shower without a swimsuit before you get in. This is taken very seriously, and a notice with a diagram is displayed in every changing room, in case anyone has doubts. I followed it carefully, and then sat in the steam while the northern lights began to flicker overhead.

I returned to Reykjavik on the tenth day, tired, sunburnt and windburnt, with a camera full of photographs and a notebook full of petrol receipts. When I told a friend that I had seen four seasons in one afternoon, he laughed and said that this was nothing special. If you plan to go, choose between the summer, when the sun hardly sets, and the winter, when the nights are long and the aurora is possible. Book your car early, buy a map and fill the tank whenever you see a station. Above all, leave some time to do nothing, because the best moments cannot be scheduled.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Губы округлены, как для «у», затем быстро раскрываются; не «в».
Кончик языка между зубами, голос включён; не «з».
Язык не касается нёба и не вибрирует; губы слегка вытянуты.
Не оглушайте конец слова: «road» оканчивается звонким «d», а не «т».

questions.question: What is the rule on one-lane bridges?
questions.answer: Whoever arrives first has the right of way.
